<reason>B's two mechanism objections survived the full exchange unanswered: a registered securities exchange cannot list the non-security assets that make up most volume (A conceded registered venues trade "almost none"), and broker-dealer customer-property/segregation rules reach securities and their cash, not Bitcoin custody — A's "the examiner sees the custody on the same page" was assertion, dismantled by "Seeing is not segregating" plus the never-answered Madoff example. B also inverted A's wheat example into proof that robust non-securities regimes deliver segregation and capital with teeth, reframing the motion correctly as a choice of box, not a choice of rules. A's strongest weighing — "protections in force beat protections in a draft" — was blunted by B's closing question "in force for whom?" A was cleaner on format (B's Rebuttal 2 was clipped) and its timing critique of bespoke statutes had real force, which keeps this competitive rather than dominant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 wheat inversion (commodity brokers are supervised as futures commission merchants, not securities broker-dealers — proving the motion's box isn't the only source of teeth) combined with Rebuttal 2's segregation-scope point that broker-dealer customer-protection rules don't cover crypto custody. A never substantively answered either, and B's closing converted them into the decisive "in force for whom?" frame.</best_rebuttal>
